How to Choose a Reputable Precious Metals Dealer
Key factors to vet a bullion dealer: reputation, licensing, transparent pricing, authentication, and red flags that signal fraud or counterfeit risk.
Choosing the right precious metals dealer is critical for your investment security. The market is crowded, and the gap between a reputable shop and a problem dealer often shows up only after money has changed hands. Knowing what to vet up front protects you from counterfeits, opaque pricing, and outright fraud.
Research Reputation and Track Record
Start with the dealer’s history in the industry. Longevity is not a guarantee of integrity, but it filters out the worst actors.
Years in business:
Look for dealers with at least 5-10 years of continuous operation.
Third-party reviews:
Check Trustpilot, Google Reviews, and bullion-specific review sites. Read the negative reviews carefully and look at how the dealer responded.
Industry memberships:
Reputable dealers often belong to organizations such as the Professional Numismatists Guild (PNG) or the Industry Council for Tangible Assets (ICTA).
Better Business Bureau:
BBB ratings and complaint histories are imperfect but useful as one data point among several.
Verify Licensing and Credentials
A legitimate dealer operates as a real business with a paper trail you can verify.
Business license:
Confirm the dealer is properly licensed in their state.
Sales tax registration:
Legitimate dealers carry the correct tax documentation for jurisdictions where they ship.
Physical address:
Be wary of dealers that only list a P.O. box or have no verifiable business location.
Staff expertise:
Look for certified coin graders or precious metals specialists on staff, especially if you plan to buy numismatic or semi-numismatic products.
Evaluate Pricing and Transparency
Premiums vary, but the way a dealer presents prices reveals a lot about how they treat customers.
Competitive premiums:
Compare premiums over spot across at least three dealers for the same product before you buy.
Clear pricing structure:
All-in pricing should be visible before checkout. Watch for hidden fees, “processing” charges, or surprise minimums.
Buy-back policies:
A reputable dealer will publish or readily quote buy-back prices. A wide gap between bid and ask is a warning.
Live pricing:
Prices should update in real time against current spot, not sit static for hours.
💡
Compare three quotes
Before any first-time purchase, get the all-in delivered price for the exact same product (e.g., a 1 oz American Gold Eagle) from three dealers on the same day. The spread tells you who is fair and who is hoping you don’t shop around.
Assess Product Selection and Authentication
Quality dealers stock authentic, widely recognized products and stand behind them.
Government-minted products:
Sovereign coins (Eagles, Maples, Krugerrands, Britannias) and bars from major refiners (PAMP, Valcambi, Royal Canadian Mint) are the easiest to verify and resell.
Authentication guarantees:
Dealers should guarantee the authenticity of every product they sell, in writing.
Return policies:
Look for a reasonable return window for defective or misrepresented items.
Storage options:
Many established dealers offer segregated or allocated storage. This is useful, but verify the custodian and audit terms separately.
Red Flags to Avoid
A few patterns repeat across nearly every bad dealer story.
High-pressure sales tactics:
Anyone telling you that you must buy today, before “the price moves,” is selling, not advising.
Bait and switch:
Beware of dealers who advertise low-premium bullion, then steer you toward “exclusive,” “limited,” or “proof” products with premiums of 30% or more over melt.
Too-good-to-be-true pricing:
Prices well below the market often indicate counterfeit product or a scam.
Poor or evasive communication:
A dealer who can’t answer basic questions about premiums, shipping, or returns is not one you want holding your money.
No physical presence:
Online-only operations without a verifiable address and phone number carry more risk than established firms.
⚠️
Numismatic upsell trap
The most common complaint against retail bullion dealers is the bait-and-switch from low-premium bullion into “rare” or “collectible” coins priced at multiples of their melt value. If a salesperson pivots away from the product you called about, end the call.
Payment and Shipping
How a dealer handles money and delivery matters as much as the price.
Payment methods:
Most reputable dealers accept bank wires and personal checks for the best pricing, with credit cards available at a small premium. Avoid anyone who demands cryptocurrency or untraceable payment for retail orders.
Fully insured shipping:
Every shipment should be insured for full replacement value.
Reasonable delivery times:
Typical delivery runs 7-14 business days after payment clears.
Tracking and signature:
Dealers should provide tracking numbers and require signature on delivery for orders above a low threshold.
Questions to Ask Before Your First Order
Use this short list on any new dealer:
How long have you been in business under this name?
What is your current buy-back price for the product I’m considering?
Do you guarantee authenticity in writing?
What are your shipping, insurance, and signature policies?
Can you provide references from long-term customers, or point to verified third-party reviews?
A dealer who answers these directly is worth your business. A dealer who deflects is telling you something useful.
For a longer treatment of the same checklist with examples, see the linked guide on
choosing a gold bullion dealer
. The fundamentals do not change: verify the business, compare premiums, and walk away from pressure.
